Funk rhythm guitar is closer to drumming than to strumming. The guitarist's hand moves
down and up on every sixteenth note, all the time. Most of those strokes make only a
click. A few of them are short, sharp chords. Which strokes sound and which are muted
is the rhythm.

Cory Wong is a well-known player of this style today. He is best known for his
clean, bright sixteenth-note rhythm guitar with the band Vulfpeck and in his own bands.
Before him there were Nile Rodgers (Chic) and Jimmy Nolen (James Brown's band). *(These
names and facts are from memory and not yet checked against a source.)*

The examples on this page are played by the site's band. Its funk guitarist uses the
two techniques this lesson teaches: **dead scratches** and **choked chords**.

## 1. The hand never stops

Count four sixteenths on every beat: **1 e & a, 2 e & a, 3 e & a, 4 e & a**. The strumming
hand goes **down** on each number and each "&", and **up** on each "e" and each "a". It
keeps going whether a stroke sounds or not. Without that steady motion, the syncopated
chords later on will not land in the right place.

Start with every stroke sounding. This is the band's plain sixteenth-note strum, with the
chords ringing:

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="funk16" data-chart="E9|E9|A9|E9" data-tempo="92" data-comp="guitar" data-choice-label="Guitar:" data-choices='[{"label":"Strummed, ringing","opts":{"compRhythm":"strum16"}}]'></div>

Keep the movement small and from the wrist. Start at half tempo.

## 2. Muting: what the left hand does

Muting is what turns a strum into funk. There are two kinds, and the fretting hand
(the left hand for most players) does both.

**The dead scratch.** Lay the fretting fingers across the strings without pressing them
down to the frets. When you strum, the strings cannot ring, and you hear a dry *chk*.
Lay the fingers flat and loose. If any string rings, you are pressing too hard or not
covering it.

**The choked chord.** Press the chord shape down for one stroke, then release the
pressure straight away. Keep the fingers on the strings. The chord sounds for a moment
and then stops. That short, sharp sound is sometimes called a *chank*.

So the left hand is always moving between *pressed* and *resting*. The right hand just
keeps strumming sixteenths. Your right palm can also rest lightly on the strings near the
bridge to quiet the low strings. That is called palm muting, but most funk muting is
done by the fretting hand.

In this example the band's guitarist chokes a chord on 2 and on 4, and scratches on every
other stroke:

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="funk16" data-chart="E9|E9|A9|E9" data-tempo="92" data-comp="guitar" data-choice-label="Guitar:" data-choices='[{"label":"Chank on 2 and 4","opts":{"compRhythm":"funkChank"}},{"label":"Strummed, ringing","opts":{"compRhythm":"strum16"}}]'></div>

Switch between the two buttons. The hand moves the same way in both. The only difference
is what the fretting hand does.

## 3. Small shapes on the top strings

Funk players seldom strum all six strings. A three- or four-note shape on the top strings
cuts through the band and leaves the low notes to the bass. A dominant ninth chord (E9, A9)
is the classic funk sound. The band's guitarist plays its funk on the top three strings.

Your shape has to be easy to press and release very quickly, so pick a small one you can
hold without effort.

## 4. Syncopated hits

Now play chords only on a few sixteenths, and scratch on all the rest. The band's
two-bar pattern is:

- **Bar 1:** chords on **1**, the **a** of 1, the **&** of 2, the **a** of 3 and the **&** of 4.
- **Bar 2:** chords on the **&** of 1, the **&** of 2, **3**, the **e** of 4 and the **a** of 4.

The chords on an "e" or an "a" are **up**strokes. That only works if the hand has kept
moving. Say the sixteenths aloud ("1 e & a ...") and say the hit syllables louder.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="funk16" data-chart="E9|E9|A9|E9" data-tempo="88" data-comp="guitar" data-choice-label="Guitar:" data-choices='[{"label":"Syncopated hits","opts":{"compRhythm":"funkScratch"}},{"label":"Chank on 2 and 4","opts":{"compRhythm":"funkChank"}},{"label":"Strummed, ringing","opts":{"compRhythm":"strum16"}}]'></div>

Use the guitar button under the example to leave the guitar out and play the part
yourself with the bass and drums. The drums play sixteenths on the hi-hat, so you can
lock your hand to them.

## 5. Your own pattern

Once the two patterns above feel easy, make up your own. Keep the hand moving and choose
two to five sixteenths in the bar for chords. A good rule is to put at least one chord on
the beat, so the band can hear where "1" is, and the rest off it.

The **Sixteenth-note funk** style on the Backing Track page plays this guitar part with
its bass line and drums, on any chord chart. Its **Comping** menu also has the chank on
2 and 4.
